title: Chapter 226 – The First Fare Answers
html:
[Terrace Seven – Jian]

The mirror will not let go of Ye Shuhan, and Jian has been standing in front of it for nineteen minutes trying to understand why.

He has tried everything that can be tried without breaking the first rule of the Terrace, which is not to answer. He has stood with his hands behind his back and looked. He has circled the iron frame. He has let the Scan open once, at the cost of an hour, and read the glass as one reads a locked door.

```
ARK-7 // SCAN (Soul band) [-1 hour]
Target: MIRROR (iron, Sect row, position 41)
Type: ACCEPTED GIFT. Subject inside: YE SHUHAN, Elder, Azure Cloud Sect.
Status: PRESENT, CONSCIOUS, RETAINED.
Gift accepted: "Your six pupils restored, whole, and your Sect's
name unstained."
Retention condition: the gift remains in force while the subject
remains in the frame.
Release condition: the gift must be ANSWERED. A debt of one
voice owed by a person who has paid.
Warning: any attempt to pull the subject out by force will
retract the gift. The six pupils will return to stone.
```

He closes the panel and lets out a slow breath.

It is a trade, he thinks. He said yes to a trade. The glass pays him as long as he stays in it.

Behind him the others have fanned out along the aisle, keeping their backs to the rows of silent blue-robed figures. Yue stands with her sword half-drawn, watching the mirrors the way a cat watches a hole in the wainscot. Hua has her mark-hand pressed to her chest. Pebble has shut his eyes. Veyra, propped against a silver column, is breathing in short shallow draws, and Corin sits at her feet with his thin arms wrapped round his knees. Nobody speaks. In the iron frame, Ye Shuhan's palm is still raised, and his lips are still shaping the same two words.

Help me. Help me.

"He can hear us," says Hua, softly.

"I know."

"Can he answer?"

"Only the way he is doing." Jian rubs his face. "The glass lets him speak. It does not let him move. He can ask for help for as long as anyone is watching. If we leave, he stops."

"Stops what?"

"Being able to ask."

Hua is silent.

---

It is the bell that gives him the idea.

He feels it before he knows what he feels: a cold flutter against his thigh, where the dead black glass of the Ferryman's bell has hung since the Fourth Terrace in a pocket of his cloak. It has been dull as a river stone for eleven weeks. It has not hummed, or warmed, or whispered. He had stopped noticing the weight of it, the way a man stops noticing a coin in his shoe.

Now it is trembling.

He draws it out. It lies in his palm, round and heavy, smaller than a plum, and in the white light of the Seventh it looks like a hole cut in the air. A thin line of pale light runs across it from edge to edge, as fine as a hair. It brightens as he watches. It pulses, once, twice, in time with his heart.

"What is it?" says Yue.

"I don't know."

"Is it the Ferryman's?"

"Yes."

"It's empty."

"It was." He turns the bell over. "Mo Yan said there was a girl in it. The first fare. She said the girl would like to see the top."

The line of light widens.

It spreads across the glass like frost across a pane, branching and re-branching, filling the dark with pale lace. The bell grows warm in his palm. It grows warmer. It begins to hum, a thin high note he can feel in his back teeth, and in the mirror beside him Ye Shuhan's face changes, the mouth opening in the beginning of a cry.

Put it down, says Veyra, hoarsely. Jian. Put it on the floor.

He kneels. He sets the bell on the black glass, and takes his hand away.

For a moment nothing happens. The bell sits upon its own reflection, a small black sphere with a halo of white fire. Then, quite gently, with a sound like a very old key turning, it opens.

It does not break. It does not shatter. It simply parts along the line of light, in two halves, like a seed splitting its husk, and from the gap between them a girl steps out.

---

She is nine years old.

She is small, and thin, and very pale, with a mop of black hair cut short around her ears and a gap where one front tooth ought to be. She wears a gray smock that comes to her knees, and her feet are bare. She stands on the black glass with her hands at her sides and her chin lifted, and looks around her, at the white ceiling, the endless mirrors, the six strangers in their dusty cloaks, with the grave, level, appraising gaze of a child sizing up a new school.

"So that's what it looks like," she says.

Her voice is clear and light and entirely unafraid.

Nobody speaks. Pebble has opened his eyes. Hua has taken half a step forward, her hand lifted, and then stopped, as one stops before a deer in a clearing.

"I'm Ilse," says the girl. "I was the first. I don't suppose you know."

The first fare, says Veyra.

"That's right. A year of my life, for the first crossing." She says it quite cheerfully. "I was nine. My mother put me on the boat. She said it was an honor." She tilts her head. "It wasn't, particularly. But it was something to do."

"Ilse," says Jian, carefully.

"You're the one who carried me." She turns her bright dark eyes on him. "I could feel you. All the way up. You were very careful. You didn't drop me once." The gap-toothed smile flashes. "I liked that."

"Thank you."

"I wanted to see the top." She glances around her. "This isn't the top. It's much too shiny."

"No."

"But it's closer." She nods. "That's all right."

She turns, quite deliberately, and looks at the iron mirror.

---

She does not walk to it. She wanders, her hands in the pockets of her smock, kicking idly at the black glass with her bare toes, and stops a pace from the frame. She looks up at the gray-haired man with the raised palm. She looks at him for a long time.

"He's very sad," she says.

"Yes."

"He said yes to something."

"Yes."

"I used to do that." She scuffs her foot. "In the boat, I mean. The Ferryman asked me if I wanted to go and I said yes, because Mother would have been cross. But I didn't." A small frown. "I didn't want to. I only said so. It's different."

Jian kneels beside her.

He does not know why. It is not a thing the Scan would recommend. But there is something in the set of the small thin shoulders that reminds him of Mo Yan, in the dust of the Quay, saying I'm here, and his knees go before he can stop them.

"Ilse," he says. "Do you know how to get him out?"

"Of course."

"How?"

"You answer it." She says it as one states the color of the sky. "He said yes. You have to say no."

"He can't say no. He's in the frame."

"Not him." She looks at Jian with a faint, tolerant surprise. "Me."

The mirror gleams.

"I'm the one who paid," says Ilse. "The first fare. I paid the Founders' bargain with my whole life, and I didn't get anything for it. Not a thing. Not even a thank-you." She tucks her hands in her pockets. "So I'm owed. That's how it works, isn't it? A thing that costs, and nothing comes back, is a debt."

That is the old law, says Veyra, very low.

"I'm going to collect," says Ilse.

"What will you ask for?"

"His no."

She turns.

She walks to the iron frame. She stands in front of it, a small gap-toothed girl in a gray smock, and puts out one hand, palm flat, and touches the glass.

---

It does not ripple.

It does something worse. It answers. Jian feels it in his stomach, a lurch, a sudden sick dropping, as when a floor gives way. The silence of the Terrace deepens. In the long rows, the blue-robed figures stir. Their closed eyes flutter. Their hands, folded in their sleeves, begin very slowly to unclench.

"Ilse!" calls Hua, sharply.

The girl does not turn.

"It's all right," she says. "It's only listening."

She leans her forehead against the glass.

"I'm Ilse," she says quietly. "I'm the first fare. I paid, and nobody thanked me. I'd like it back."

What would you ask? says the mirror.

It speaks aloud. Its voice is soft, beautiful, grave, and sorrowing, the voice of a woman who has loved a great many people and lost all of them. It comes from everywhere. It comes from the glass beneath their feet. It makes Jian's eyes sting.

What would you ask, little one? A mother? A garden? A name?

"No," says Ilse.

A life?

"I've had one."

A brother?

"I never had one."

Then what?

"I'd like him to stay out," says Ilse. She says it with the careful clarity of a child reciting a lesson. "The man in the frame. He said yes to a gift. I'd like to give it back. I'd like to say, on his behalf, that he didn't mean it. That he's sorry. That he was tired, and sad, and it was a very long time, and it's not fair to hold a person to a promise made in the dark."

The mirror is silent.

That is not a debt, it says at last.

"It's mine."

A first fare does not owe the glass.

"I'm not a fare any more," says Ilse. "I'm just a girl. And I'd like him to have his no."

The silence stretches.

Jian does not breathe. He is aware of Yue's hand on her hilt, of Hua's lips moving, of Corin's wide shocked eyes. He is aware of the thin hot line of light running across the black glass of the bell at his feet, widening and widening, until it is no longer a crack but a seam, and the whole of the little dark sphere is splitting, flaking, falling away in ashes.

It is costing her, says Veyra.

"I know."

She is paying with the bell. The cool voice breaks. She is paying with the last thing she has.

Jian is on his feet before he knows it.

"Ilse!"

She does not look back.

---

The mirror shatters.

It does not do so with a crash. It does it gently, softly, in a long falling ripple, like a pane of ice breaking up in spring. The iron frame stays upright. The glass within it dissolves into drifting white motes, thousands of them, which rise in a slow glittering column to the ceiling and vanish. And from the empty frame a man steps out.

He is sixty. He is gray. He wears a pale blue robe and a brown traveler's cloak, thick with dust, and his hands are shaking so badly that he cannot hold them still. He takes one step. He takes another. His knees fold, and he goes down on the black glass in a heap of blue and brown, and he does not rise.

"Elder Ye!" cries Hua.

She is beside him before anyone else has moved. She kneels, and gets an arm under his shoulders, and lifts his head against her knee. His face is the color of tallow. His eyes are open. They are brown, and wet, and fixed on the white ceiling, and they do not blink.

"Six," he says.

His voice is a husk.

"Six pupils. I left them. I left them on the Quay." A rattling breath. "I said yes to a gift. I said, if the Sect's name could be saved, and the six restored. I said yes."

"Hush," says Hua.

"They are stone. They are still stone. I know it. I felt it when the glass broke. The gift is gone." He turns his head, and sees her, and his face crumples. "I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I should never have gone up."

"They are not stone."

"I felt—"

"Lan Xiu woke them," says Hua, gently. "Thirty years ago, in the world below. With the Cartographer's book, and a hundred pupils of your Sect. Pei laughed. She said Lan Xiu had got fat."

Ye Shuhan stares at her.

"Thirty years," he says.

"More like seventy. The Terraces run fast."

"They woke."

"They woke."

"They are alive."

"Yes."

He makes a sound, deep in his chest, that Jian will remember for a long time. It is not a sob. It is not a laugh. It is the sound of an old man setting down a weight he has carried for a lifetime, and finding that his arms do not know how to stop reaching.

Hua holds him.

She does not say anything more. She sits on the black glass in the white light, with a stranger's head in her lap and her own mark glowing gold on her palm, and the others stand round them in a ragged ring, and the long rows of blue-robed figures stir and sigh and fall still.

---

Ilse is gone.

Jian sees it last. He has been so intent on the man in the frame that he has not looked at the girl, and when he does, there is nothing to look at. The black glass of the floor is bare. The two halves of the bell lie where they fell, a few paces from the shattered frame, dull and cracked and empty. There is no small figure in a gray smock. There is no gap-toothed smile.

There is only, on the black glass, a faint warm print, the shape of a small bare foot, fading.

He kneels.

He picks up the halves of the bell, and holds them in his hand. They are light. They are lighter than he remembers, as though something that weighed upon them for six centuries had at last been set down.

Ilse, he thinks.

The panel appears, very quietly, at the edge of his vision. He does not want to read it. He reads it.

```
ARK-7 // NOTE
Entity "Ilse" (first fare): DISCHARGED.
She paid the debt of the glass with the last of the bell and
the last of herself. She is not dead. She is not here.
Destination: unknown. Probability she reached "the top":
not computable.
Note: the Seventh Terrace has lost one of its locks. The mirrors
are weaker for 60-90 minutes. This is the best window you
will have.
```

He closes the panel.

The best window you will have, he thinks bitterly. She just died, and the machine is reading me a schedule.

But he has learned, over many lives, that grief is a thing that can be carried and walked with at the same time. He tucks the halves of the bell into the pocket of his cloak. He rises. He turns to the others.

"We have an hour," he says.

---

They carry Ye Shuhan between them.

He cannot walk. His legs, long folded under him, will not straighten, and he weighs no more than a bundle of sticks. Pebble takes his shoulders and Corin his feet. They go down the long aisle in single file, past the rows of silent blue-robed figures, and nobody looks at the glass.

"I should tell you," Ye Shuhan says, in a thin cracked voice, somewhere in the second mile, "what I learned."

"You don't have to."

"I do." His eyes are closed. "I have been in the frame for a long time. I do not know how long. It does not matter. But in that time I heard things, through the glass. I heard the Terraces. I heard the Door."

"Tell me," says Jian.

"The Tenth is not a man." The old Elder's mouth works. "I thought he was. I climbed the whole Road thinking he was a god in a high place, and I walked into the Door and found nothing but a chair. A chair, and a ring of light, and a voice coming out of the air."

Jian's skin crawls.

"A voice."

"It spoke to me. It said it had been waiting for someone like me. It said I was good, and brave, and the Sect's finest son." A shudder runs through the thin frame. "It said it would give me anything. Anything at all. And I said, my pupils. And it said, of course."

"And then?"

"And then I was in the mirror." He opens his eyes. They are brown and bleary and terribly clear. "It was not Orrin Thann. He was there, at the Door. I could see him. A man in a chair, with his back to me, very thin, very still. But he was not the one who spoke. I do not think he could. I think he had been silent for a very long time."

"Silenced."

"Held." Ye Shuhan's mouth trembles. "Like a bird in a hand."

Nobody speaks.

At the head of the line, Yue has stopped dead. She stands in the aisle with her stone hand raised, a tall thin figure with a white streak in her hair, and when she turns her face is the color of ash.

"The stair," she says.

They look.

At the end of the long aisle, perhaps a hundred paces away, a gap opens in the rows of mirrors. A narrow stair of black stone, steep and bare, climbs into darkness. At its foot there is a small iron bowl, set into the wall, and in the bowl, shining like stars, five grains of salt.

That is the way up, says Veyra, weakly. To the Eighth.

"And the way back down?" says Hua.

The old woman does not answer.

---

They rest at the foot of the stair, because there is nothing else to be done.

Pebble makes a bed of two cloaks. Hua feeds the old Elder bread and water, a mouthful at a time, and he takes them like a sick child, with his thin throat working and his eyes fixed on her face. Corin sits nearby, with his arms round his knees, and does not speak. Veyra has sunk to the floor with her back against the wall and her eyes shut. Her breathing is slow and shallow and she has not moved in a quarter of an hour. Jian sits beside her, and says nothing, and holds the two cracked halves of the Ferryman's bell in his steady hand.

Yue stands at the lip of the stair with her sword drawn, watching the aisle.

"Tell me about the Door," she says, without turning.

Ye Shuhan swallows. He sets down the cup. "It is a round room," he says. "White. With a roof of glass. I stood there for a time that I cannot measure, and I could see the sky through the roof. It was a bad sky. Torn, and pale, and running with fire."

"The Seam."

"Yes." His thin hands knot in his lap. "In the middle of the room there was a ring of seats. Nine of them. Carved from a single stone. Eight were empty." He closes his eyes. "In the ninth there was a man."

"Orrin."

"I did not see his face. He had his back to me. He wore a gray robe, and his head was bowed, and his hands lay on the arms of the chair. They were thin. They were thinner than anything I have ever seen." A shudder. "And on the back of the right hand there was a mark. A circle, with a gap. It was glowing. It was the only light in the room."

Veyra has opened her eyes.

Describe the hand, she says.

"My lady?"

Describe it. Is it open or closed?

"Open." He frowns. "Palm down on the arm of the chair. The fingers curled a little. As if—" He stops. "As if it were waiting for someone to put something into it."

Yes, says Veyra. That is how he held it, when he was thinking. Her voice is very faint. He would sit by the fire with his hand open on his knee, like a man waiting for a coin.

Nobody speaks.

"And the voice?" says Jian.

"It came from above." Ye Shuhan lifts his face to the white ceiling. "Not from the room. From the glass. From the sky. It was warm and quiet and exactly like a man I had known as a boy. My old master, who taught me the sword." His mouth twists. "I wept. I could not help it. It said my name. It said, Shuhan, you have done so well."

Hua takes his hand.

"I knew it was wrong," he says. "I knew, even then. A god does not need to say well done. A god does not ask for anything. But I wanted to hear it so much." The tears run down his seamed face. "I have wanted to hear it for forty years."

"We all do," says Hua, quietly.

"It was the cruelest thing it could have said."

"It was the kindest."

"It was both," says Jian.

They look at him.

He is still looking at the cracked halves in his hand. "That is how it works," he says. "It finds the one true thing you most want to be told, and it says it. And then it takes the rest."

---

The fare is paid at the iron bowl, one grain at a time.

Jian goes last. He stands with the five grains in his palm, and thinks of the arithmetic: ninety years, two hundred and twelve days; less one for each of five. He takes up the first grain, and holds it between thumb and forefinger. It is cold. It is small. It is very bright.

He hands it to Yue.

She takes it without a word. She does not look at it. She closes her stone hand over it, and the grain vanishes, and she sways, once, with a small sharp breath, and straightens.

Hua takes the second. Pebble takes the third. Ye Shuhan, who cannot stand, is helped to the bowl by Corin and Pebble, and takes the fourth in a trembling hand, and says, in a voice like dry reeds: "A year. For the pupils."

The fifth is Jian's.

He lifts it. He holds it to the white light. He thinks, for no reason at all, of a small gap-toothed girl in a gray smock, standing on a boat, saying yes when she meant no.

I will not do that, he thinks. I will not say it unless I mean it.

He closes his hand.

The tick comes, as before, small and dry, like a watch losing a tooth. He feels the year go. It leaves nothing behind but a faint chill under the breastbone, and the knowledge that somewhere in the world below, a seventh part of a century has passed in the time it takes to draw breath.

```
ARK-7 // LEDGER
Fare paid: Terrace Seven -> Terrace Eight. Passengers: 5.
Lifespan: 90y 212d -> 89y 212d
Outside time since gate: 74 years (est.).
Note: the Eighth Terrace has no published time ratio.
The Founders' register records one word beside it: "ONE."
```

One, he thinks.

One to what?

He does not know. He puts the question aside, and helps Pebble lift the old Elder, and turns to the stair.

It is narrow and steep and black. It rises into a darkness that seems to breathe. Above it, very faintly, he can hear a sound he has not heard since the Hall of Ten Thousand Names: the dry rustle of paper, a vast soft whispering, as of ten thousand scrolls being turned at once.

"Ready?" says Yue.

"No," says Jian.

"Good." She sheathes her sword. "Neither am I."

They climb.
